commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources endorse incident response plans for AI failures, drift, or nonconforming outputs, and one FDA draft guidance frames nonconforming-product control as a manufacturer requirement. No supplied study tests whether such plans shorten harm or improve outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base consists of nine endorsements: one draft guidance, three frameworks, one multi-society statement, and four commentaries. No comparative, observational, or case-series study was supplied. Under GRADE conventions, the effect of incident response plans on time to detection, harm duration, or patient outcomes cannot be rated, and agreement among sources reflects expert opinion rather than tested effect.

The FDA draft guidance ties AI device oversight to existing quality-system duties to control nonconforming product, which gives manufacturers a regulatory basis for procedures. For health systems, the radiology multi-society statement, CHAI, NIST AI 600-1, and HEAAL use should-level language. A Korean legal commentary proposes postevent review by a designated safety officer with reporting to authorities.

The sources name the elements they expect in a plan: notification, a defined mode of operation while the model is under assessment, severity classification, auditable escalation records, and a designated lead. No supplied study shows which of these elements catches errors before they reach patients or how quickly a plan contains harm once drift is detected.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study tests incident response plans for clinical AI, and no supplied study measures how often uncoordinated responses prolong harm. Useful designs would include before-and-after or interrupted time-series studies across sites that adopt plans. These could measure time from drift detection to containment, the number of patients exposed to nonconforming outputs during the interval, and the fidelity of interim operation such as fallback to manual workflows. Simulation or tabletop exercises could also report which plan elements fail under realistic conditions.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. HEAAL and the Arabic-language triage commentary raise equity-relevant settings but offer no data. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether incident plans reach patients who may be less likely to report problems or to receive notifications in their language.
